title: Graceful rewind and merge for late-arrival SSE events and tool-call boundary safety
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Goal: Implement a server-side 'rewind-and-merge' capability for SSE clients that receive out-of-order or late fragments, while guaranteeing that function/tool calls are not executed multiple times and structured outputs remain consistent. This feature should reduce application-visible glitches when network hiccups or client reconnects cause fragments to arrive after a reconnection window.

Background: We've seen customer incidents where streaming clients reconnect and receive delayed fragments that should logically attach to previously emitted events (e.g., multi-part tables, JSON structures, or function-call arguments). Existing strategies (simple drop, naive replay, or full resume token reconstitution) either lose useful tokens, risk duplication of side-effects (tool calls), or add large state transfer costs. We need a middle ground: bounded rewind with deterministic merge semantics and explicit tool-call commit boundaries.

Non-goals: This ticket is not implementing a fully general CRDT for arbitrary outputs, nor does it change the public resume token format. It is focused on improving server-side handling for short-late fragments (seconds to low minutes) and providing a safe contract for tool-calls and structured outputs.

Design proposal summary:
1) Fragment metadata: Every SSE chunk emitted by the runtime will carry the following lightweight metadata fields (in the event payload headers): fragment_id (UUID v4), seq (monotonic integer per-stream), parent_seq_hint (optional integer), boundary_type (one of: content, commit, tool-boundary), and span_checksum (short rolling hash). These are appended to structured JSON events in the existing event stream shape.

2) Rewind window: Server maintains a per-connection sliding 'rewind window' (configurable, default 12s) that keeps last N fragments and their metadata. If a reconnect occurs with a resume token that indicates a position inside the window, the server will allow the client to request a 'rewind-and-merge' which attempts to merge late fragments by seq into the previously delivered stream.

3) Merge rules:
  - idempotence: fragments with the same fragment_id are dropped if already observed.
  - ordering: seq numbers are used to place late fragments; if parent_seq_hint is present, it will guide attachment for structured outputs.
  - conflict resolution: for overlapping content fragments touching the same logical output slot, the server prefers the fragment with later server-received timestamp unless the fragment has a commit boundary that was already applied; in that case, the commit wins and late fragments are discarded.

4) Tool-call safety: Tool invocation events are emitted as two-phase markers: tool-call-intent (tool-boundary) and tool-call-commit. The runtime will only forward the actual invocation to the external tool backend on tool-call-commit. If a reconnect causes duplicate intent events, they will be coalesced and never cause a duplicate external call. Only a commit event transitions the call to executed. This requires maintaining a short-lived tool-call registry keyed by tool-call-id (UUID). The registry is ephemeral and scoped to the rewind window; if the registry entry expires (beyond rewind window) the call is considered lost and clients must re-issue.

5) Structured output stitching: For JSON or quoted-structure outputs (function call args, JSON blobs), fragments carry a structural hint (e.g., path like /choices/0/message/content/0) to allow safe reassembly instead of blind concatenation. This reduces corruption when late fragments represent interior pieces of a JSON value.

6) API contract and backwards compat: The public resume token remains unchanged; we extend the streaming event payload with backward-compatible metadata fields inside a namespaced key so older clients ignore them. New SDK versions will opt-in to request rewind-and-merge during reconnect if the token indicates an in-window resume.

Trade-offs and considerations:
  - Memory vs correctness: keeping a rewind window costs memory on hosts; we bound it and recommend small defaults. Dedicated/Dedicated-High customers can configure larger windows.
  - Tool-call registry lifetime: too short => risk loss; too long => increased resource consumption and possible privacy concerns. We selected default 12s, tunable per-tenant.
  - Complexity: Adds server-side merging code paths and more metadata; we mitigate by keeping metadata minimal and using existing observability hooks.

Rollout plan:
  - Phase 1 (dev & unit tests): implement fragment metadata, in-memory rewind buffer, and deterministic merge logic behind feature flag. Add unit + fuzz tests for boundary cases (overlaps, duplicate fragments, partial JSON).
  - Phase 2 (canary): enable on 1% of traffic in hosted runtime for non-critical models (no external tool integrations). Monitor stream reassembly success rate and API error increase.
  - Phase 3 (tool-safe): enable tool-call two-phase commit for canary customers that opt in. Work with a small set of partners to validate no duplicate tool executions.
  - Phase 4 (general availability): promote to 100% with opt-in per-tenant controls and admin knobs for window size and commit timeouts.

Metrics to monitor: merge_success_rate, merge_conflicts_per_minute, tool_call_commits, tool_call_duplicate_attempts, stream_reconnects, average_rewind_memory_bytes. Target: merge_success_rate > 99.5 and tool_call_duplicate_attempts == 0 for opt-in customers.

Open questions:
  - Should the server allow client-directed merge priorities (client can signal prefer-late or prefer-original)? For now we keep server-side deterministic rules.
  - What is the UX for the SDK when a tool-call was lost because registry expired? Proposal: SDK surface returns a specific error code and helper to replay intent.
  - Long-term: should we expose a streaming-level CRDT for collaborative use-cases? Out of scope for this ticket.

Testing and QA:
  - Unit tests for fragment dedup, ordering, conflict resolution.
  - Integration test using a simulated flaky network that reorders fragments and reconnects mid-stream.
  - End-to-end test that hooks into a mock external tool verifying single execution semantics.

Artifacts and links:
  - Design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/REWIND+and+Merge+Design (internal)
  - Spike PR demonstrating in-memory buffer and merge logic: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1489
  - Prototype test harness for fuzzing reassembly: https://github.com/redwood-inference/stream-tests/tree/rewind-fuzz

Next steps: finalize metadata field names and wire them into event codec, land basic buffer and test harness, open canary rollout PR with feature flag gating.
